paper.title: PDDFormer: Pairwise Distance Distribution Graph Transformer for Crystal Material Property Prediction
paper.research_summary: The paper introduces WPDDFormer and UPDDFormer—graph transformer models that integrate atom-weighted and unit-cell pairwise distance distribution (PDD) representations into multi-edge crystal graphs—to achieve continuous and geometrically complete crystal structure representations for improved property prediction. It addresses discontinuity and ambiguity in traditional crystal graph representations caused by atomic vibrations and lattice non-uniqueness, and demonstrates state-of-the-art accuracy on Materials Project and JARVIS-DFT benchmarks.

tasks.objective: Predict scalar physical properties of crystalline materials from their 3D atomic structure
input_requirements: 3D crystal structure (unit cell, atomic positions, atomic types, lattice vectors)
output_goal: scalar property values (e.g., eV/atom, eV, GPa)

evidence.text: Comprehensive evaluation results show that WPDDFormer achieves state-of-the-art predictive accuracy across tasks on benchmark datasets such as the Materials Project and JARVIS-DFT.
We conducted experiments on two material benchmark datasets, namely the Materials Project [Chen et al., 2019] and Jarvis [Choudhary et al., 2020] datasets.

stages.stage_goal: Construct continuous and geometrically complete multi-edge crystal graphs using WPDD or UPDD
stage_output: WPDD crystal graph G = (X, XI, E, WPDD)
UPDD crystal graph G = (X, XI, E, UPDD)

evidence.text: By introducing PDD, we constructed a general complete and continuous multi-edge crystal graph. In the graph, node features are xi. An edge is established from node j to node i when the Euclidean distance |ej′i|2 between a duplicate of j and i satisfies |ej′i|2 = |pj + k′1l1 + k′2l2 + k′3l3 −pi|2 ≤r, where r ∈R is the cutoff radius. Next, we construct a PDD row for each atom. Since directly representing PDD as edge features is impractical, we retain its matrix form and incorporate it into the construction of the multi-edge crystal graph to reflect the global information of the crystal structure. Therefore, we represent the constructed crystal graph as G = (X, XI, E, PDD).

evidence.text: Finally, we employ the Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) [Rubner et al., 2000] to assess the continuity of crystal graphs, demonstrating that WPDD crystal graphs constructed using only Euclidean distances maintain continuity and general completeness under slight atomic position perturbations, providing a more accurate depiction of actual crystal structures.
